slides.title: Classifying rejection from kidney biopsy RNA
paragraphs: This project asks a specific question: once a kidney transplant biopsy has been collected, can its molecular measurements classify the rejection diagnosis recorded for that tissue?
actions: Pause after the research question, then move to the biopsy diagram.

slides.title: Kidney biopsy and transplant rejection
paragraphs: A kidney transplant gives a person a donor kidney. The recipient's immune system can recognize it as foreign and attack it. That immune response is rejection.

A biopsy is a small tissue sample. Follow the two branches. A specialist examines thin sections under a microscope for injury and inflammation. Histology means studying tissue this way, and it supplies the study's recorded diagnoses.
The other branch contains molecular measurements from the tissue. Those become the model inputs. The recorded diagnosis supplies the answer used to train and evaluate the classifier.
These are two kinds of evidence from tissue already collected. That raises the practical question: if we have the microscope assessment, why measure the molecules as well?
actions: Trace the tissue sample into the microscope and molecular-measurement branches.
Point to the two-kinds-of-evidence caption, then introduce the question answered on the next slide.
visible_cues: Rejection: immune attack on a donor kidney
Biopsy tissue: a small tissue sample
Two kinds of evidence from tissue already collected

slides.title: Molecular support for uncertain biopsies
paragraphs: The proposed use is a molecular second opinion for biopsies that are difficult to interpret. A biopsy may show borderline changes, or its appearance may conflict with other clinical findings. A specialist then needs to weigh the available evidence.

Histology shows tissue appearance. RNA messages give information about gene activity in that tissue. These are different kinds of evidence from a biopsy already collected. A molecular assessment could add information for specialist review.

This project takes an early step toward that use: learn rejection-related molecular patterns from recorded diagnoses, test how well they agree, and build reproducible scoring software. The intended value is helping with uncertain interpretation. Whether this particular score adds that value needs direct evaluation.
actions: Begin by answering why molecular measurements could matter after a biopsy exists.
Follow tissue appearance and gene activity into specialist review.
Point to the project contribution before moving to the external evidence.
visible_cues: Possible use: a molecular second opinion
Uncertain interpretation: borderline findings or clinical disagreement
Project: learn rejection patterns from recorded diagnoses

slides.title: Evidence for a molecular second opinion
paragraphs: There is a clinical research basis for this proposal. Banff guidance, which supports the classification of transplant biopsy findings, considers validated molecular tests in selected difficult cases.

Rosales and colleagues used B-HOT, the same set of RNA measurements used in this project. Patients who later developed chronic active antibody-mediated rejection, a form caused by immune proteins called antibodies, had higher initial rejection-related molecular scores as a group, despite lacking that diagnosis on their initial biopsy.

That supports the idea that RNA can add information beyond the initial tissue interpretation. The future-outcome finding belongs to that external study. This project tests classification of recorded diagnoses. Its added value for uncertain biopsies is the next question to evaluate.
actions: Distinguish the clinical guidance from the independent B-HOT study.
Name the external study before describing its later-outcome result.
End at the distinction between current classification and proposed added-value evaluation.

slides.title: Recorded diagnoses
paragraphs: The study records four diagnoses. Antibody-mediated rejection involves antibodies, proteins made by the immune system. T-cell-mediated rejection involves T cells, a type of immune cell. Mixed rejection includes both processes.

Those three categories all count as rejection here. The fourth, no rejection, supplies the comparison group. That does not necessarily mean healthy tissue. It means the recorded diagnosis is outside those rejection categories.
The classifier answers a two-category question: rejection or no rejection. We retain the original diagnoses to examine which kinds it misses.
actions: Read down the diagnosis table, then point to the common rejection label.
visible_cues: T-cell-mediated: T cells are immune cells
No rejection does not necessarily mean healthy

slides.title: Measuring RNA in biopsy tissue
paragraphs: RNA includes the messages cells make when genes are expressed. Counting those messages tells us which genes are active and how much RNA is present in the tissue.
An assay is a laboratory test. This study uses NanoString nCounter with the B-HOT panel. A panel is the fixed list of molecules the assay measures.
Probes recognize selected RNA molecules. Identifying barcodes let the instrument count their signals. Each named measurement becomes a number in the specimen's record.
IFNG is one of those measurements. In the public specimen we'll follow through the application, its raw count is four. This is how RNA becomes a number the analysis receives.
actions: Follow RNA, probe recognition, barcode counting, and the IFNG example in order.
Point to the IFNG count of 4. Treat the assay diagram as an illustration.
visible_cues: RNA: gene messages in the tissue
Probes recognize selected RNA; barcodes identify counted signals
Panel: a fixed list of measurements

slides.title: The measurements used by the model
paragraphs: Each specimen has 770 measurements. Of these, 758 describe RNA signals that become model inputs. Some measure viral RNA, so they include more than human genes.
The other 12 are housekeeping measurements. They provide a reference for preparing the counts, then are removed. The model receives the 758 prepared inputs.
An assay target means the molecule a probe recognizes. I'll use measurement for an input and recorded rejection for the outcome.
These counts describe tissue. A larger count can reflect greater activity within cells, a different mixture of cells, or both.

slides.title: Preparing counts for the model
paragraphs: First, add one to each raw count and take its base-two logarithm. Adding one allows zero counts. The logarithm compresses the range of values.
IFNG has a raw count of four. Four plus one is five, and its base-two logarithm is about 2.322.
Transform the specimen's 12 housekeeping measurements in the same way and average them. Here, that reference is about 7.900. Subtracting it from 2.322 gives a prepared IFNG value of minus 5.578.
Repeat that subtraction for all 758 RNA measurements. Each is now relative to its specimen's reference level. The housekeeping measurements are then removed from the inputs.

This calculation uses only the specimen being scored, without its diagnosis or other specimens. Further preparation learned from data, such as logistic regression's input scaling, is fitted on training specimens only and reused unchanged.
actions: Walk down the example calculation, including the plus one before the logarithm.
Point to the 12-reference average and the final 758 inputs.

slides.title: Development and evaluation specimens
paragraphs: The study authors supplied two groups, or cohorts: 1,050 discovery specimens and 345 technical-validation specimens. This project preserves that division.

A saved discovery split assigns 787 specimens to training and 263 to screening, keeping the four diagnosis proportions similar. Training fits the model. Screening compares candidates and chooses the threshold for a rejection flag.
The separate 345 specimens evaluate the selected procedure. All four models use those same rows. The fitted model and its threshold remain together, without refitting before evaluation.
These roles show which data influence each decision. The authors call the second group technical validation. The records do not establish that it contains entirely different patients or centers.
actions: Trace 1,050 into 787 training and 263 screening, then point to the separate 345 branch.
Use the source term technical validation and state the patient/center limit.

slides.title: Four model comparisons
paragraphs: The constant model gives every specimen the training rejection fraction as its score. It shows what happens without RNA measurements.
The IFNG model uses the one measurement we've already seen, testing how much information it provides alone.
Logistic regression combines measurements with learned weights. Regularization restricts those weights to limit fitting the training data too closely.
CatBoost combines decision trees. Each tree asks a sequence of questions about measurement values. Together they can represent more complicated relationships.
All four use the same specimens and preparation. Does combining measurements help, and does CatBoost improve enough over logistic regression to justify its complexity?
actions: Move through the four models in the displayed order.
Finish at the shared rows and preparation cue.
visible_cues: Constant: same training rejection fraction for everyone
Logistic regression: weighted combination; regularization restricts weights

slides.title: Turning a score into a rejection flag
paragraphs: A threshold turns the model score into a flag: scores at or above it count as rejection. A recorded rejection below it is a miss. A no-rejection specimen at or above it is a false flag.
Screening chooses a threshold retaining at least 90 percent of recorded rejection cases, then minimizing false flags.
CatBoost keeps its threshold of approximately 0.876588 for evaluation and the application. The 90 percent rule is an experimental choice, not a clinical requirement or guarantee elsewhere.
Threshold selection does not establish reliable individual probabilities. The application therefore calls the output a model score.
actions: Point to the threshold before naming misses and false flags.
Point to the frozen threshold and the model-score label.
visible_cues: Score at or above threshold becomes rejection flag
Screening rule: retain at least 90%, then minimize false flags
Model score; probability calibration is a separate question

slides.title: Several measurements reduced false flags
paragraphs: Here are the results on the 345 evaluation specimens. The two colors distinguish the errors: how many of the 169 recorded rejection specimens were missed, and how many of the 176 no-rejection specimens were falsely flagged? Keep those two denominators in mind as we compare the models.

The constant model flags every specimen at its fixed threshold. It misses zero of 169 rejection specimens, but falsely flags all 176 of 176 no-rejection specimens. That shows why detection alone cannot tell us whether a model is useful.
The IFNG-only model misses 14 of 169 rejection specimens and falsely flags 75 of 176 no-rejection specimens. It detects many rejection cases, but it also produces many false flags.
The full-panel logistic model misses 33 of 169 rejection specimens and makes eight false flags among 176 no-rejection specimens. CatBoost misses 25 of 169 and also makes eight false flags among 176.

Compared with IFNG, CatBoost makes 67 fewer false flags but misses 11 more rejection cases. Both parts of that tradeoff matter. The threshold rule chosen in development leads to different error counts in this evaluation group.

Compared with logistic regression, CatBoost detects eight more rejection specimens with the same false-flag count. Combining measurements helps reduce false flags here. The smaller difference between the two full-panel models needs closer examination before we treat it as a dependable advantage.
actions: Read the rejection and no-rejection denominators before the chart.
Explain the constant-model caption, then the IFNG bars at the bottom, logistic bars in the middle, and CatBoost bars at the top.
Pause on the IFNG tradeoff and the eight-case difference from logistic.
visible_cues: CatBoost versus IFNG: 67 fewer false flags, 11 more misses

slides.title: Most CatBoost misses were T-cell rejection
paragraphs: The original diagnoses help us examine CatBoost's 25 misses: six of 56 antibody-mediated specimens, 18 of 95 T-cell-mediated specimens, and one of 18 mixed specimens.

T-cell rejection accounts for most misses and is the largest rejection group. About 19 percent was missed, compared with about 11 percent of the antibody-mediated group. One miss among only 18 mixed specimens gives limited evidence about what to expect elsewhere.

Overall, the model detects 144 of 169 rejection specimens, or 85.2 percent. This fraction is sensitivity. On screening, it detected 157 of 174, or 90.2 percent. Evaluation falls below the 90 percent threshold-selection rule.

The screening rule therefore cannot guarantee performance on new specimens. These errors are disagreements with recorded diagnoses. Resolving individual disagreements would require tissue and clinical-record review.
actions: Point to each miss count with its denominator.

slides.title: The advantage over logistic regression is uncertain
paragraphs: CatBoost detects eight more of 169 rejection specimens than logistic regression. Each makes eight false flags among 176 no-rejection specimens. How dependable is that difference?

Resampling repeatedly draws from these specimens, allowing repeats. Both models use the same draws. The 95 percent interval for their detection difference includes zero. This holds the models fixed and does not establish patient independence.

A separate check repeats development with 20 saved discovery splits. Each separates fitting, screening, and assessment. The selection rule chooses CatBoost in 13 repetitions and logistic regression in seven.
The repetitions overlap, showing variation with the split. The demonstration retains frozen CatBoost. Logistic regression remains a credible simpler comparison for the next cohort.

Move to the separate 13-of-20 and 7-of-20 follow-up.

slides.title: Training and serving share the same preprocessing
paragraphs: Training and prediction use the same preparation code. A CSV enters through the command line or web application. Both routes check the measurements, normalize each specimen, and call the configured model.
The response contains specimen ID, model score, frozen threshold, rejection flag, and model version. The version identifies the saved model. The flag records whether the score crossed its threshold.

The service loads the project-controlled model. Callers submit counts, not replacement models. Missing measurements, duplicate names, negative counts, and non-finite values cause explicit errors instead of a score.
The reliability analysis did not establish trustworthy individual probabilities across the score range. The application presents a model score alongside the threshold that gives its flag meaning.

slides.title: Next evidence for a molecular second opinion
paragraphs: We now have measured agreement with recorded diagnoses in one study and working scoring software. The next step connects that result to the proposed use.

A new cohort should include patient and center identifiers and documented assay quality. Here, assay groups are linked to cohort membership, so their effects cannot be cleanly separated. Numeric file checks also do not establish laboratory quality.

Fix the models and thresholds beforehand, including logistic regression. On uncertain biopsies, compare usual assessment with assessment plus the molecular score. Use independent expert review and follow-up outcomes to judge whether it improves interpretation.
That comparison tests the intended added value of a molecular second opinion. It is the next research step, supported by the prototype developed here.

slides.title: Molecular counts can classify recorded rejection
paragraphs: CatBoost missed 25 of 169 rejection specimens and made eight false flags among 176 no-rejection specimens. Its advantage over logistic regression remains uncertain.

Shared prediction code, explicit input errors, and inspectable evidence make this a tested research prototype for molecular support of biopsy interpretation. Next, test its added value on uncertain biopsies in a new cohort.

backups.title: Backup: complete primary comparison
paragraphs: This table keeps the four models on the same 345 evaluation specimens. Miss counts use the 169 recorded rejection specimens. False-flag counts use the 176 recorded no-rejection specimens. Sensitivity is the fraction of rejection specimens flagged, and specificity is the fraction of no-rejection specimens left unflagged.

CatBoost has 85.2 percent sensitivity and 95.5 percent specificity, compared with 80.5 and 95.5 percent for logistic regression. IFNG detects a larger fraction of rejection specimens, at 91.7 percent sensitivity, but its specificity is 57.4 percent. The constant baseline flags everyone.

ROC-AUC describes how well scores rank rejection above no rejection across possible thresholds. CatBoost has ROC-AUC 0.969, logistic regression 0.956, IFNG 0.842, and the constant baseline 0.500. The error counts describe each model at its frozen threshold.
actions: Answer the requested metric question by pointing to its table column. Keep both class denominators visible.

backups.title: Backup: normalization and threshold selection
paragraphs: For each specimen, the normalized measurement equals log base two of its raw count plus one, minus the mean log base two of the 12 housekeeping counts plus one. Every required measurement must be present. The reference comes from that specimen alone.

Logistic regression also scales its inputs using quantities learned only from training rows. Its regularization setting is C equals 0.1. The selected CatBoost model uses 300 trees with depth four and learning rate 0.04. These settings describe the saved comparison.

The screening rule chooses thresholds retaining at least 90 percent of screening rejection specimens and minimizing false flags. Both models detected 157 of 174 rejection specimens. Among 89 no-rejection specimens, CatBoost falsely flagged five and logistic regression six. This screening comparison selected CatBoost.

The frozen service flags scores at or above 0.8765880870219778. It retains the fitted model used to choose that threshold. Refitting the model would require a compatible threshold-selection procedure.
actions: Use the formula for preparation questions, the model-settings text for configuration questions, and the screening counts for selection questions.

backups.title: Backup: ranking does not guarantee calibrated scores
paragraphs: This reliability plot groups evaluation specimens into ten fixed score ranges. For each range, it compares the average model score with the fraction of specimens recorded as rejection. Agreement with the diagonal would mean that those two quantities match in that range.

In the highlighted range from 0.8 to 0.9, the mean score is 0.847. Seven of the 16 specimens have recorded rejection, or 43.8 percent. The displayed 95 percent interval for that fraction runs from 23.1 to 66.8 percent. The group is small, and this range was highlighted after inspecting the plot.

A model can rank specimens well without producing reliable probabilities in each score range. No calibration model was fitted on the evaluation data. The application therefore calls its output a model score.
actions: Keep the bin count visible when describing a gap.
Do not interpret 0.876588 as a proven 87.7 percent individual risk.

backups.title: Backup: subtype follow-up retained the binary service
paragraphs: This follow-up compared models trained on the four diagnoses with the original model trained on rejection versus no rejection. The table converts each result to the same any-rejection question, using discovery-selected rules, so the displayed error counts are comparable.

The binary CatBoost benchmark misses 25 of 169 rejection specimens with eight false flags among 176 no-rejection specimens. Four-class CatBoost misses 29 with eight false flags, and four-class logistic misses 28 with ten false flags. The separate antibody and T-cell component models miss 24 with 15 false flags. That last approach finds one additional rejection case while adding seven false flags.

The four-class logistic model correctly identifies ten of 18 mixed diagnoses and makes five false mixed calls among 327 non-mixed specimens. That is a separate subtype question from the binary counts in the table.
The follow-up supplied no reason to replace the frozen binary service. Because this evaluation cohort had already been examined, these findings require confirmation in a new cohort.
actions: Explain the any-rejection conversion before comparing table rows.
Point to the separate mixed-diagnosis sentence only when discussing subtype recognition.

backups.title: Backup: study, assay and deployment limits
paragraphs: The recorded metadata does not confirm patient or transplant-center independence. Biopsy-level resampling may therefore give uncertainty intervals that are too narrow if some specimens are related.

The software checks required measurements and usable numeric counts. The project did not independently repeat laboratory quality checks such as control-probe or imaging checks. Assay compatibility and completed laboratory quality checks remain requirements for a meaningful input.

The score reliability analysis does not establish trustworthy individual probabilities, so the service labels its output a model score. The local research container has been tested. Cloud deployment remains deferred.
actions: Answer the relevant row of the limitations table, then use the specimen-resampling note if asked about uncertainty.

backups.title: Backup: sources and contributions
paragraphs: Zhang and colleagues supplied the public study and the GSE212160 deposit. This project uses their raw measurements for its own binary comparison. It does not reconstruct the authors' published classifier.

The project provides its own saved model runs, shared software, and a tested local demonstration. Configurations, input hashes, reports, and source code allow another person to inspect the quantitative claims.

The presentation guide draws on Bourne for audience and rehearsal, Kosslyn and colleagues for presentation flaws, Garner and Alley for connecting slide statements to evidence, and Rougier and colleagues for clear figures. AI assisted with preparing this presentation.
actions: Describe the presenter's actual contribution when asked; do not infer earlier personal work from repository authorship.
Keep full linked references available in the HTML speaking guide.

backups.title: Backup: UNOS research connection
paragraphs: UNOS researchers have studied whether artificial intelligence can identify anatomical issues from donor-kidney photographs. They used historical transplant and refusal records to label the images. The stated aim includes supporting clinical decisions and making anatomical assessment more consistent.

The connection is the research approach: learn from existing assessments to develop an additional source of evidence for transplant professionals. In this project, the inputs are RNA measurements and the question concerns rejection in biopsy tissue.
The UNOS example addresses a different clinical task. It provides relevant context for this approach, without endorsing this project or establishing that our classifier improves clinical decisions.
actions: Explain the historical labels and intended assessment support before drawing the connection.
Keep the distinct clinical tasks explicit.
